claim: 68% of the 663 million cases of malaria prevented since 2000 have been through the use of long-lasting insecticide treated bednets (LLINs).
source: It is estimated that 68% of the 663 million cases of malaria that have been prevented since the year 2000 have been through the use of long-lasting insecticide treated bednets (LLINs) (Bhatt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhatt et al., 2015, which provides the quantitative estimate.

claim: Mosquitoes show widespread resistance to pyrethroids in Africa.
source: However, there is a growing realisation that insecticide resistance is putting these advances under threat (WHO, 2012), with mosquitoes reporting widespread resistance to pyrethroids, the only class of insecticides currently approved for use in bednets (Ranson and Lissenden, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2012 and Ranson and Lissenden, 2016.

claim: Pyrethroids are the only class of insecticides currently approved for use in bednets.
source: However, there is a growing realisation that insecticide resistance is putting these advances under threat (WHO, 2012), with mosquitoes reporting widespread resistance to pyrethroids, the only class of insecticides currently approved for use in bednets (Ranson and Lissenden, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ranson and Lissenden, 2016.

claim: The public health impact of pyrethroid resistance in areas of LLIN use is hard to quantify due to multiple epidemiological factors.
source: The public health impact of pyrethroid resistance in areas of LLIN use is hard to quantify as a comparison between sites is complicated by multiple epidemiological factors making it difficult to ascribe differences in malaria metrics solely to mosquito susceptibility (Kleinschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kleinschmidt et al., 2015.

claim: Experimental hut trials are time consuming, relatively expensive, and geographically limited.
source: These experiments are time consuming, relatively expensive, and geographically limited and by themselves they do not fully account for all effects of the LLIN as they do not show the community impact (herd effects) caused by the insecticide killing mosquitoes (Killeen et al., 2007; Magesa et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations to Killeen et al., 2007 and Magesa et al., 1991.

claim: Experimental hut trials do not fully account for community impact (herd effects) caused by insecticide killing mosquitoes.
source: These experiments are time consuming, relatively expensive, and geographically limited and by themselves they do not fully account for all effects of the LLIN as they do not show the community impact (herd effects) caused by the insecticide killing mosquitoes (Killeen et al., 2007; Magesa et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Killeen et al., 2007 and Magesa et al., 1991.

claim: There are no easy to use genetic markers that can reliably predict the susceptibility of mosquitoes to pyrethroid insecticide.
source: There are no easy to use genetic markers that can reliably predict the susceptibility of mosquitoes to pyrethroid insecticide (Weetman and Donnelly, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weetman and Donnelly, 2015.

claim: Bioassays measure mosquito mortality after exposure to a fixed dose of insecticide.
source: The current most practical phenotypic method for assessing resistance is the use of bioassays which take wild mosquitoes and measures their mortality after exposure to a fixed dose of insecticide (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2013a.

claim: The discriminating doses used in bioassays are unrelated to field exposure.
source: However the discriminating doses used in the assay are unrelated to the field exposure and so the predictive value of these bioassays for assessing the problems of pyrethroid resistance is unknown.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Insecticide treated bednets still outperform untreated nets in experimental hut trials even against pyrethroid resistant populations.
source: A meta-analysis has shown that insecticide treated bednets still outperform untreated nets in experimental hut trials even against pyrethroid resistant populations (Strode et al., 2014) though the community impact (herd effects) of the LLIN was not assessed (Killeen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strode et al., 2014.

claim: The population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance is changing at a fast rate.
source: The population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance is known to be changing at a fast rate (Toé et al., 2014) making it important to regularly re-evaluate the efficacy of LLINs in order to guide current vector control and resistance management strategies (WHO, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Toé et al., 2014.

claim: PBO LLINs are substantially better at killing insecticide resistant mosquitoes in some locations but not others.
source: Studies have shown that PBO LLINs are substantially better at killing insecticide resistant mosquitoes in some locations but not others (Ngufor et al., 2014a, 2014b; Kitau et al., 2014; Asale et al., 2014; Ngufor et al., 2014c; Koudou et al., 2011; Corbel et al., 2010; Tungu et al., 2010; Malima et al., 2008; Adeogun et al., 2012a; Agossa et al., 2014; Malima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: PBO LLINs are more expensive than standard LLINs, with one manufacturer's 2012 price for PBO LLIN being US$4.90 compared to US$3.25 for a comparable standard LLIN.
source: PBO LLINs are more expensive than standard LLINs, with one manufacturer's 2012 price for PBO LLIN being US$4.90 compared to a comparable standard LLIN price of US$3.25 (Briët et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim provides specific pricing data supported by a citation to Briët et al., 2013.

claim: PBO LLIN (PermaNet 3.0) was cost effective compared to a threshold of US$150/DALY averted in 4 of 6 sites studied.
source: It predicted that the more expensive PBO LLIN was still cost effective compared to a threshold of US$150/DALY averted (not comparing against standard LLINs) in 4 of the 6 sites, though these results are not generalisable beyond the specific sites chosen by the manufacturer, population prevalence of resistance, the type of LLIN or mosquito species.
evidence: The claim is based on modeling results from a previous study.

claim: Mosquito mortality in a bioassay can predict the proportion of mosquitoes which die in experimental hut trials.
source: Meta-analysis M1 shows that mosquito mortality in experimental hut trials can be predicted by the percentage of mosquitoes surviving a simple pyrethroid bioassay (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from meta-analysis M1 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a substantial association between pyrethroid resistance in a bioassay and mortality measured in a standard LLIN experimental hut trial.
source: There is a substantial association between pyrethroid resistance in a bioassay and mortality measured in a standard LLIN experimental hut trial (Figure 2A, Deviance Information Criteria, DIC, with resistance as an explanatory variable = 2544.0, without = 2649.0 (lower value shows more parsimonious model), best fit parameters α1 = 0.634 (95% Credible Intervals, 95%CI, 0.012–1.29) and α2 = 3.99 [95%CI 3.171–5.12]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (DIC values) and model parameters shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For the A. gambiae complex, PBO has the greatest benefit in mosquito populations with intermediate levels of pyrethroid resistance.
source: Data suggests that for the A. gambiae complex PBO has the greatest benefit in mosquito populations with intermediate levels of pyrethroid resistance (including pyrethroid resistance as an explanatory variable DIC = 2544.0, without DIC = 4748.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (DIC values) from meta-analysis M2.

claim: In A. funestus, adding PBO appears to kill all mosquitoes irrespective of the prevalence of pyrethroid resistance.
source: In A. funestus adding PBO appears to kill all mosquitoes irrespective of the prevalence of pyrethroid resistance (including resistance as an explanatory variable improved model fit, with DIC = 2544.0, without DIC = 2547.0, though the gradient of the line was so shallow as to effectively make the PBO synergised pyrethroid mortality independent of the population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (DIC values) from meta-analysis M2.

claim: The number of mosquitoes deterred from entering the experimental hut substantially decreases in areas of higher pyrethroid resistance.
source: Figure 3A indicates that the number of mosquitoes deterred from entering the experimental hut substantially decreases in areas of higher pyrethroid resistance (where LLIN induced mortality inside the hut is low) though the variability around the best fit line is high suggesting the precise shape of the relationship is uncertain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As the population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance increases, an increasing proportion of mosquitoes entering the house exit without blood-feeding.
source: As the population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance increases (and mortality inside the hut decreases) an increasing proportion of mosquitoes entering the house exit without blood-feeding (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only when there is very high population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance does the probability that a mosquito will successfully feed start to increase.
source: Only when there is a very high population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance does the probability that a mosquito will successfully feed start to increase (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Washing decreases LLIN efficacy fastest in areas of higher pyrethroid resistance.
source: Results indicate that washing decreases efficacy fastest in areas of higher pyrethroid resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental hut trial data with washed nets.

claim: Mosquitoes with high pyrethroid resistance appear to overcome the insecticide activity of the LLIN faster than susceptible mosquitoes.
source: Mosquitoes with high pyrethroid resistance appear to overcome the insecticide activity of the LLIN faster than susceptible mosquitoes.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of decay in pyrethroid activity shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The higher the population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance, the greater impact it will have on both the number of clinical cases and the force of infection.
source: The transmission dynamics model predicts that the higher the population prevalence of pyrethroid resistance the greater impact it will have on both the number of clinical cases (Figure 4A and B) and the force of infection (as measured by the EIR, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on predictions from the transmission dynamics model shown in Figures 4A, B, and C.

claim: With 30% resistance (70% mortality in discriminating dose assay) in a population with 10% slide prevalence, pyrethroid resistance would cause an additional 245 (95%CI 142–340) cases per 1000 people per year.
source: For example with as little as 30% resistance (70% mortality in discriminating dose assay) in a population with 10% slide prevalence (in 2–10 year olds) the model predicts that pyrethroid resistance would cause an additional 245 (95%CI 142–340) cases per 1000 people per year (Figure 4A, averaged over the 3 year life-expectancy of the net).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative predictions from the transmission dynamics model with confidence intervals.

claim: In an area with 10% endemicity and 80% resistance (20% mortality in discriminating dose assay), switching to PBO LLINs would avert an additional 501 (95%CI 319–621) cases per 1000 people per year.
source: For example in an area with 10% endemicity and 80% resistance (20% mortality in discriminating dose assay) the model predicts that switching to PBO LLINs would avert an additional 501 (95%CI 319–621) cases per 1000 people per year (Figure 5A) compared to the same level of standard LLIN coverage.
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative predictions from the transmission dynamics model with confidence intervals.

claim: The absolute number of cases averted by switching to PBO LLINs is predicted to be greater in areas with intermediate endemicity.
source: The absolute number of cases averted by switching to PBO LLINs is predicted to be greater in areas with intermediate endemicity as human immunity is likely to partially buffer the added benefit of PBO LLINs in areas of highest malaria prevalence (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 5B and includes reasoning about human immunity.

claim: The greatest percentage reduction in clinical cases and EIR is seen in areas of low endemicity.
source: However, due to the non-linear relationship between incidence of clinical infection and endemicity, the greatest percentage reduction in clinical cases and EIR is seen in areas of low endemicity (Figure 5CF).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions shown in Figures 5C and 5F.

claim: The bioassay is a crude tool for measuring pyrethroid resistance.
source: The bioassay is a crude tool for measuring pyrethroid resistance, though its simplicity makes it feasible to use on a programmatic level.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the nature of the bioassay tool.

claim: On average, bioassay mortality is able to predict the results of standard and PBO LLIN experimental hut trials for A. gambiae s.l. mosquitoes.
source: Figure 2A and C indicate that on average bioassay mortality is able to predict the results of standard and PBO LLIN experimental hut trials for A. gambiae s.l. mosquitoes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: There is a high level of measurement error in the bioassay.
source: There is a high level of measurement error in the bioassay (as seen by the wide variability in points in Figure 2A and B) so care should be taken when interpreting the results of single assays as differences in mosquito mortality may have been caused by chance.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation of variability in Figures 2A and B.

claim: The probability that a mosquito will feed on someone beneath an LLIN only increases substantially at high levels of pyrethroid resistance.
source: This analysis suggests that the probability that a mosquito will feed on someone beneath an LLIN only increases substantially at high levels of pyrethroid resistance (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental hut trial data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: People under bednets exposed to mosquito populations with intermediate levels of resistance still have a high degree of personal protection whilst in bed.
source: People under bednets exposed to mosquito populations with intermediate levels of resistance still have a high degree of personal protection whilst in bed as those mosquitoes, which do not die are likely to exit the hut without feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing mosquito behavior at intermediate resistance levels.

claim: It is only when mosquito populations are highly resistant (>60% survival) that an increasing proportion of mosquitoes appear to successfully feed through the LLIN.
source: It is only when mosquito populations are highly resistant (>60% survival) that an increasing proportion of mosquitoes appear to successfully feed through the LLIN (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim provides a specific threshold (>60% survival) based on data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The loss of deterrence suggests that those sleeping in a house with an LLIN though not sleeping under the net themselves will lose an additional degree of protection.
source: Importantly the loss of deterrence suggests that those sleeping in a house with an LLIN though not sleeping under the net themselves (a phenomenon particularly common in older children [Nankabirwa et al., 2014]) will lose an additional degree of protection (on top of the community impact of mosquito killing).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed loss of deterrence and includes a citation about net usage patterns.

claim: Repeatedly washing a net appears to have little impact on its ability to kill a susceptible mosquito whilst significantly reducing the lethality of the LLIN against more resistant mosquitoes.
source: Repeatedly washing a net (and presumably reducing the concentration of the insecticide) appears to have little impact on its ability to kill a susceptible mosquito whilst significantly reducing the lethality of the LLIN against more resistant mosquitoes (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of washed net data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Even at low levels of pyrethroid resistance, the loss of insecticide activity over the three year bednet life-expectancy has a bigger epidemiological impact on malaria than the initial efficacy of new LLINs.
source: Nevertheless the results seem to be confirmed by two recent studies which evaluated mosquito mortality in older (standard) LLINs (Toé et al., 2014; Wanjala et al., 2015). Durability studies should be prioritised as the model predicts that, even at low levels of pyrethroid resistance, the loss of insecticide activity over the three year bednet life-expectancy, has a bigger epidemiological impact on malaria, than the initial efficacy of new LLINs.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and supported by citations to Toé et al., 2014 and Wanjala et al., 2015.

claim: Even low pyrethroid resistance can increase the number of malaria cases over the life-time of the net at a population level.
source: Though a person under an LLIN requires high pyrethroid resistance before LLINs start to fail (Figure 3C), the models predict that at a population level even low pyrethroid resistance can increase the number of malaria cases over the life-time of the net (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions shown in Figures 3C and 4A.

claim: The loss of LLIN induced mosquito mortality is likely to decrease the community impact of LLINs, increasing average mosquito age and the likelihood that people are infected whilst unprotected by a bednet.
source: The loss of LLIN induced mosquito mortality is likely to decrease the community impact of LLINs, increasing average mosquito age and the likelihood that people are infected whilst unprotected by a bednet.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model results about community-level effects.

claim: Detecting an epidemiological impact of a low population prevalence of resistance may be challenging for local health systems.
source: Detecting an epidemiological impact of a low population prevalence of resistance may be challenging for local health systems (for example, see < 20% resistance prevalence Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4) especially in an area where LLIN coverage, local climatic conditions and the use of other malaria control interventions are changing over time.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model results shown in figures.

claim: A mosquito population is defined as being pyrethroid resistant if there is < 90% bioassay mortality.
source: Currently a mosquito population is defined as being pyrethroid resistant if there is < 90% bioassay mortality (WHO, 2013b; Mnzava et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2013b and Mnzava et al., 2015.

claim: The personal protection provided by sleeping under an LLIN is likely to be substantial even at very high levels of resistance.
source: The personal protection provided by sleeping under an LLIN is likely to be substantial even at very high levels of resistance (Strode et al., 2014; Randriamaherijaona et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strode et al., 2014 and Randriamaherijaona et al., 2015.

claim: Any reduction in mosquito mortality will likely reduce the community impact of LLINs though it may be hard to detect, especially in areas with new LLINs.
source: Any reduction in mosquito mortality will likely reduce the community impact of LLINs though it may be hard to detect, especially in areas with new LLINs (the public health impact of resistance is likely to be greater in older nets, Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model results and data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In A. funestus, PBO always appears to restore near 100% mortality.
source: In A. funestus PBO always appears to restore near 100% mortality whilst for mosquitoes from the A. gambiae complex the greatest additional benefit of PBO being seen at intermediate levels of pyrethroid resistance (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on bioassay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PBO's primary synergistic effect of pyrethroids is thought to be due to the inhibition of the cytochrome P450 enzymes which catalyse the detoxification of the insecticides.
source: PBO's primary synergistic effect of pyrethroids is thought to be due to the inhibition of the cytochrome P450 enzymes which catalyse the detoxification of the insecticides (Farnahm, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farnahm, 1998.

claim: Elevated P450 levels are the primary resistance mechanism in A. funestus.
source: Elevated P450 levels are the primary resistance mechanism in A. funestus whereas in A. gambiae s.l. both increased detoxification and alterations in the target site contribute to pyrethroid resistance with the latter mechanism being largely unaffected by PBO (Mulamba et al., 2014; Riveron et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mulamba et al., 2014 and Riveron et al., 2013.

claim: In A. gambiae s.l., both increased detoxification and alterations in the target site contribute to pyrethroid resistance.
source: Elevated P450 levels are the primary resistance mechanism in A. funestus whereas in A. gambiae s.l. both increased detoxification and alterations in the target site contribute to pyrethroid resistance with the latter mechanism being largely unaffected by PBO (Mulamba et al., 2014; Riveron et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mulamba et al., 2014 and Riveron et al., 2013.

claim: Target site alterations contributing to pyrethroid resistance are largely unaffected by PBO.
source: Elevated P450 levels are the primary resistance mechanism in A. funestus whereas in A. gambiae s.l. both increased detoxification and alterations in the target site contribute to pyrethroid resistance with the latter mechanism being largely unaffected by PBO (Mulamba et al., 2014; Riveron et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mulamba et al., 2014 and Riveron et al., 2013.

claim: Both bioassay and hut trial data suggest a minimal additional benefit of PBO in areas with very high levels of pyrethroid resistance for A. gambiae s.l. populations.
source: For A. gambiae s.l. populations this result was verified by experimental hut trial data which directly compare standard and PBO LLINs (Figure 2C). Both bioassay and hut trial data suggest a minimal additional benefit of PBO in areas with very high levels of pyrethroid resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on data from bioassays and experimental hut trials shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The WHO recommends that countries routinely conduct non-PBO pyrethroid bioassays as part of their insecticide resistance management plan.
source: The WHO recommends that countries routinely conduct non-PBO pyrethroid bioassays as part of their insecticide resistance management plan (WHO, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2012.

claim: Areas with 40–90% survival (10–60% mortality) in a non-PBO standard bioassay should consider conducting PBO synergism bioassays to determine the suitability of PBO LLINs.
source: Areas with 40–90% survival (10–60% mortality) in a non-PBO standard bioassay (of any type) should consider conducting PBO synergism bioassays to determine the suitability of PBO LLINs.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: If both net types cost the same and resistance has been detected, then PBO LLINs should always be deployed as evidence suggests that they are always more effective.
source: If both net types cost the same and resistance has been detected then this work indicates that PBO LLINs should always be deployed as evidence suggests that they are always more effective.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Switching to more expensive PBO LLINs may cause a reduction in overall bednet coverage in situations where malaria control budgets are fixed.
source: In many situations, malaria control budgets are likely to be fixed and therefore switching to more expensive PBO LLINs may cause a reduction in overall bednet coverage.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about budget constraints.

claim: Much of the debate over the impact of pyrethroid resistance on LLIN effectiveness has focused on the loss of personal protection provided by new nets and does not fully take into account their community impact.
source: Much of the debate over the impact of pyrethroid resistance on LLIN effectiveness has focused on the loss of personal protection provided by new nets and does not fully take into account their community impact.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of the scientific debate.

claim: A large body of evidence has shown how widespread use of LLINs can cause considerable community protection, both to those who use bednets and non-users.
source: A large body of evidence has shown how widespread use of LLINs can cause considerable community protection, both to those who use bednets and non-users (Killeen, 2007 and references therein).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Killeen, 2007 and references therein.

claim: High levels of pyrethroid resistance are likely to have a bigger public health impact than previously thought and could represent a major threat to malaria control in Africa.
source: The evidence presented here suggests that high levels of pyrethroid resistance are likely to have a bigger public health impact than previously thought and therefore could represent a major threat to malaria control in Africa.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Meta-analysis M1 identified 21 data-points from 13 studies where concurrent bioassays and experimental hut trials were carried out.
source: Meta-analysis 1 (M1) identified only 7 studies where concurrent bioassays and experimental hut trials were carried out (Table 3).
evidence: The claim provides specific numbers from the meta-analysis, with details in Table 3.

claim: New bednets provide substantial personal protection until high levels of resistance.
source: New bednets provide substantial personal protection until high levels of resistance, though protection may wane faster against more resistant mosquito populations as nets age.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the study's findings.

claim: Protection may wane faster against more resistant mosquito populations as nets age.
source: New bednets provide substantial personal protection until high levels of resistance, though protection may wane faster against more resistant mosquito populations as nets age.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the study's findings on net durability.

claim: Even low levels of resistance would increase the incidence of malaria due to reduced mosquito mortality and lower overall community protection over the life-time of the net.
source: Transmission dynamics models indicate that even low levels of resistance would increase the incidence of malaria due to reduced mosquito mortality and lower overall community protection over the life-time of the net.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and based on transmission dynamics model predictions.

claim: Switching to PBO bednets could avert up to 0.5 clinical cases per person per year in some resistance scenarios.
source: Switching to PBO bednets could avert up to 0.5 clinical cases per person per year in some resistance scenarios.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and based on model predictions.
